## Course information

The primary aim of this course is to help you develop a solid foundation in
basic genetics so that you will be able to apply this knowledge to understand
new and emerging discoveries in the field and evaluate how these discoveries
have shaped our understanding of plant evolution, ecology and can be used for
crop improvement.

The course material ranges from classical (transmission) genetics to plant
molecular and quantitative genetics, genomics, and epigenetics. Because we
will cover a broad range of topics, this will limit the extent to which we
can explore any particular field in depth.

One theme throughout the course is how plant biology and genetics are
interconnected. Another theme is that the development of new molecular tools
has significantly advanced our understanding of genetic mechanisms. They have
provided new ways to speed up plant breeding, which is essential to ensuring
global food security.

This course emphasizes critical thinking, problem-solving and the synthesis
of information: grades are not determined by memorizing facts. The
prerequisite for PLS 152 is BIS 2A, and the class is taught accordingly.
Students who have mastered BIS 101 may find some of the initial lectures
basic, but this changes as the quarter progresses, and the core concepts
become more complex. There are many additional opportunities for advanced
students to be challenged at every stage of the course.

We may have to reframe our goals depending on how much progress we make, but
wherever possible, we will take your perspective into account.

## Course format: in person

PLS 152 is taught in person in Veihmeyer Hall 212, Tuesdays and Thursdays
from 3:10 to 5:00 PM. Although the registrar lists a lecture plus a separate
20-minute discussion, we meet as one continuous block with a short break in
the middle — plan for the full 3:10–5:00.

I hope you actively participate in this course because I have found it is the
best way to engage you in learning. Slides are posted on this website before
each class, but some of the best days of the quarter only happen in person: a
greenhouse tour, guest panels, in-class activities, and discussions. If
something prevents you from attending, contact me and we will work out how
you can keep making progress.

**Where things live:** all course materials — schedule, slides, readings,
assignment details — are on this website. Canvas is where you submit things
(quizzes, reflections, assignments) and where every deadline is listed.

## Learning outcomes

By the end of this course, students should be able to:

- Explain various ways in which plant biology affects genetic diversity and
  inheritance (dominance, meiosis, recombination, mating systems, mutation)
  and how genetic variation affects plant biology (how variation in DNA
  sequence affects plant traits).
- Interpret results from plant genetics research, including reading primary
  research articles.
- Apply knowledge of plant genetics to real-world problems in agriculture.
- Appreciate plant genetics memes.

## Prerequisites and materials

Students should have completed BIS 2A or an equivalent course covering the
fundamental concepts of molecular biology and genetics. Students looking to
refresh their knowledge are encouraged to use freely available resources,
including non-conventional ones such as YouTube and Wikipedia. If you come
across a concept or term that you don't know, sometimes a simple Google
search can be really effective.

There is no required textbook. Assignments are submitted via Canvas. Each
week pairs a primary research article with the lecture material (see
[readings](readings.qmd)) — quiz questions draw on them, and learning to read
real papers is part of the point. Bring a laptop on Thursday October 15 (the
library session and midterm work day).

## Assignments and assessment

**Class participation (10%):** a short reflection on each class, submitted on
Canvas and graded for completion, due by 11:59 PM the same day. Two
questions, every time: what interested you most today, and what would you
benefit from a deeper explanation of? I read these, and they shape the
following lectures.

**Weekly assignments (30%):** low-stakes quizzes on Canvas covering the
previous week's material, due Tuesdays at 3:10 PM, before class. Each quiz
includes at least one question drawn from that week's research article. The
lowest weekly assignment score is dropped automatically.

**Midterm (30%):** a written mini literature review on a plant genetics topic
of your choice — maximum 1,500 words, at least 5 peer-reviewed sources, due
Tuesday November 10 at 3:10 PM. The full prompt, including guidance on
choosing a topic, is on the [midterm page](midterm.qmd). The October 15
library session launches your literature search, and the Topic Explorer
(due October 22) helps you pick your topic with evidence instead of
guesswork. Midterms are graded anonymously against a rubric posted with the
assignment.

**Capstone project (30%):** the final for this class is a group presentation
(5–10 minutes) exploring a plant genetics topic — presentations run December
1 and 3. Groups form from a preference survey (due October 29), with two
short check-ins along the way. Grading is based on a rubric covering the
presentation's content and quality, plus each member's individual
contribution statement.

**Extra credit (up to 2%):** memes! Post an original genetics meme to the
class gallery by Friday December 11 — 1 point, or 2 if it's plant genetics
specific. A proud course tradition.

## Grading policy

Your success in this class is important to me. We will all need
accommodations because we all learn differently. If there are aspects of this
course that prevent you from learning or exclude you, please let me know as
soon as possible. Together we'll develop strategies to meet both your needs
and the requirements of the course.

**"Time Banks" late assignment policy:** students have a two-day grace period
for one assignment or two one-day extensions for two different assignments.
Additional late work is eligible for 60% of original points. Time Banks do
not apply to the final project (a scheduled presentation) or to daily
reflections — a reflection on today's class only makes sense today; the
completion grading and drop-lowest rules are the built-in slack. For
extraordinary circumstances (e.g. illness, emergency), please contact me as
soon as possible to make arrangements.

## Use of AI

AI tools are part of how modern science gets done, and this course will teach
you to use them: the October 15 library session covers AI research assistants
for finding and understanding scientific literature. You are welcome to use
AI to search for papers, get unstuck on a concept, test your understanding,
or get feedback on your writing.

What you submit must be your own work. Do not turn in writing generated by
AI. For the midterm in particular: every citation must be a real paper that
you actually found and read. AI tools regularly invent convincing-looking
citations, and a fabricated citation in your midterm is an academic integrity
violation, not a technology accident. You are accountable for everything you
submit, whatever tools helped along the way.

## Academic integrity

All members of the UC Davis community benefit from an environment of trust,
honesty, fairness, respect, and responsibility. You are expected to present
your own work and acknowledge the work of others in order to preserve the
integrity of scholarship. This includes submitting your own original work,
proper citation of all sources of information, keeping quiz content to
yourself, and not submitting work completed for another class without prior
permission. Violations of the Academic Integrity policy can result in
dismissal from the university and a permanent notation on a student's
transcript. For the full policy, see the Academic Misconduct page at the
Division of Undergraduate Education.

## Accessibility

Talk with me as early in the quarter as possible to explain your needs and
discuss any concerns. Solutions that benefit one student can help the whole
class, so please let me know any questions or suggestions. Contact the
Student Disability Center for more information and to request accommodations:
(530) 752-3184 · sdc@ucdavis.edu · [sdc.ucdavis.edu](https://sdc.ucdavis.edu/).

## Student wellness

You deserve respect, and are encouraged to practice self-care so that you can
remain focused and engaged; that might mean getting a drink of water, leaving
to use the restroom, taking a moment to stretch, or doing something else you
need to do to take care of yourself.

College life can be overwhelming at times, but know that you are not alone if
you're feeling stressed. Please remember to practice self-care and reach out
for support if and when you need it. You can visit
[Virtual UC Davis](https://virtual.ucdavis.edu/) to find resources related to
health and well-being, academics, basic needs (food and housing) and more.
